sections.name: Heart Container (Heart)
sections.card:
Summary: A healing item that lowers the damage percentage of whoever picks it up. In the first game it is called simply Heart, and it recovers all of your damage, taking you down to 0%.
Uses: It spawns above the ground and floats down slowly, so in the first game players have to fight over the spot where it will land. Once it is grabbed it keeps healing even if you are hit while it works.
Tips: The item list calls it the strongest recovery item. Taking enough of them in one match earns the Heartthrob bonus, worth 17,000 points in the first game (8,000 in the Japanese version).

sections.name: Maxim Tomato
sections.card:
Summary: A red tomato with a black M on it that lowers the damage percentage of whoever picks it up. In the first game it restores a full 100% of your damage; the later games only restore 50%.
Uses: In the first game any damage you take while it is healing you is ignored. Maxim Tomatoes do not spawn on Hyrule Castle.
Tips: Taking enough Maxim Tomatoes in one match earns the Vegetarian bonus, worth 9,000 points in the first game (5,000 in the Japanese version). If every item except the Maxim Tomato is turned off, any containers that fall onto the stage will be empty.

sections.name: Starman (Super Star)
sections.card:
Summary: A star that bounces around the stage and makes whoever touches it invincible for ten seconds. The first game calls it the Starman; the name Super Star came in later games.
Uses: It bounces on the field and off platforms and walls in large arcs, and it can fall off the stage if nobody grabs it in time. Touching an opponent while invincible does not damage them. The fighter sparkles, and a special music theme replaces the stage music until the effect wears off.
Tips: On Planet Zebes it makes you immune to the acid, so you can walk through it, but if you fall off the stage while invincible you self-destruct because the acid will not bump you back up. In the first game it is the one item without the small triangular marker above it.

sections.name: Beam Sword
sections.card:
Summary: A glowing sword, often called the lightsaber, that you swing for stronger hits or throw at opponents. The game's own manual says it has the longest range of all the clobbering items when thrown.
Uses: While you hold it, your neutral attack, forward tilt, dash attack and forward smash become item swipes. In the first game they deal 12%, 18%, 16% and 25%.
Tips: Thrown, it does between 13% and 20% depending on the throw. If you are hit while holding it you may drop it: in the first game the chance is the attack's damage divided by 60, so a 6% hit gives a 10% chance.

sections.name: Home-Run Bat
sections.card:
Summary: A wooden bat that turns your forward smash into a single delayed swing that can knock an opponent out in one hit.
Uses: The swing always takes a set time and cannot be charged. In the first game it uses each fighter's normal item swing, and the wind-up differs by fighter: Link is quickest at 23 frames, while Mario, Luigi and Ness are slowest at 30.
Tips: It does most of its damage with the tip of the bat rather than the middle. It is also strong when thrown, doing around 20% damage with high knockback, and swung normally it can KO fairly early, especially with a dash attack or smash throw.

sections.name: Hammer
sections.card:
Summary: A close-range item: whoever grabs it swings it back and forth non-stop, and in the first game each hit does 30% damage with very high knockback.
Uses: While you hold it you keep swinging, and you cannot jump in midair, use other attacks or defend. You cannot drop it on purpose; only being sent tumbling makes you let go. It can chain into itself for 60%, which will likely KO.
Tips: The item list calls it one of the most feared items for its range, damage and knockback, but its wielder cannot use special moves or jump in the air, so knocking them off a ledge while they swing can KO them. Careful hitbox placement can also interrupt the swing.

sections.name: Ray Gun
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range laser gun that holds 16 shots. In the first game each shot does 10% electric damage with vertical knockback.
Uses: You can fire one shot every 30 frames, and the blasts have infinite horizontal range. Like other shooting items it replaces your neutral attack, and once it is empty it only shoots blanks.
Tips: The shots can be reflected or absorbed, and the gun itself can only be reflected when thrown. In the first game you cannot move while firing it: firing while walking only arrived in Brawl.

sections.name: Bob-omb
sections.card:
Summary: A bomb with two little legs and a wind-up key on its back. Thrown at an enemy it explodes with large damage and knockback, but if it is left alone it lights its own fuse and starts walking around.
Uses: Pick it up and throw it at an opponent. It can also hurt the thrower, and it explodes if it is simply hit by an attack.
Tips: If nobody picks it up, it stands up and walks back and forth on the platform it spawned on, turning around at edges, and explodes if it walks into a fighter. If it meets nobody it blows itself up after a while.

sections.name: The 1P Game's final boss
sections.card:
Summary: The final boss of the 1P Game, fought in stage 11 on Final Destination. It cannot be cleared by knocking it past the edge of the stage; you have to use up its 300 hit points.
Weak points: Master Hand cannot be launched out of the blast zones and takes no knockback from your attacks, so the only way to win is to deplete his 300 hit points. Once he has under 100 HP left, his Finger Bullet attack fires three pairs of Bullet Bills instead of one.
Looks like: A large, gloved hand.
Tips: Side Punch hits for 20% and punches across the stage, Big Swipe hits for 16% and slaps across the platform, and Floor Sweep sweeps across the stage several times at 12% a swipe. Power Punch hovers over you, then quickly punches down with electric effects.

sections.name: Metal Mario
sections.card:
Summary: A sub-boss you fight in stage 9 of the 1P Game, only on the Meta Crystal stage. He rarely flinches, resists grabs and throws at low damage, and his attacks knock you back harder than normal.
Weak points: He can take roughly 200% damage before he can be launched (it scales with the difficulty), but he is exceptionally vulnerable to edge-guarding: once he is knocked off the stage, his extreme falling speed badly hurts his recovery. An 8-frame jumpsquat also makes his aerial attacks slow.
Looks like: At first glance he looks like an alternate costume of Mario.
Tips: He never dashes and rarely jumps, pacing across the stage at a steady walk. On lower difficulties he is passive and mostly attacks when he is interrupted, and his aggression and knockback rise on higher settings. His AI is simple, largely walking left and right and occasionally attacking.

sections.name: Giant Donkey Kong
sections.card:
Summary: A giant Donkey Kong fought on Kongo Jungle in stage 6 of the 1P Game, where two regular-sized computer partners fight alongside you.
Weak points: He can take up to around 300% damage before he can be launched, and his hits have extra knockback, plus extra reach because of his size. That size also makes him a bigger target, and his AI can be exploited so that he walks back and forth on the top platform, though your partners jumping into him or attacking him often break that pattern.
Looks like: Donkey Kong with a much larger body.
Tips: Keep your partners safe: neither being KO'd gives the DK Defender bonus (10,000 points, 7,000 in the Japanese version), and neither being damaged at all gives the DK Perfect bonus (50,000 points). On higher difficulties he acts more like a level 9 computer player while your partners are lower level.

sections.name: Fighting Polygon Team
sections.card:
Summary: Thirty weak purple polygon copies of the twelve fighters, fought in stage 10 of the 1P Game on Duel Zone, never more than three at a time.
Weak points: They are light and can usually be beaten in a single blow, though they get heavier and stronger on higher difficulties. They have no special moves, which hurts their recovery, and they cannot grab. They are passive, mostly walking around the platforms and very rarely attacking.
Looks like: Blocky, shiny purple figures that mostly keep the shape of the fighter they copy.
Tips: They pick up items and normally throw a throwing item as soon as they have it. In the bonus stage Race to the Finish they are much more aggressive, chasing you and slowing you down, and you cannot defeat them there.

sections.name: Hyrule Castle's tornadoes (stage hazard)
sections.card:
Summary: Four tornadoes spawn at random over Hyrule Castle, the stage where Link is the first opponent of the 1P Game, and a fighter caught in one is thrown upward.
Weak points: You can still attack a fighter who is caught in a tornado, and hit them with an aerial when they are released, even meteor smashing them back into the tornado for more damage.
Tips: Each lasts around 10 to 20 seconds, drifts in a random direction and may suddenly speed up and home in on a fighter. Someone caught is held for about two seconds, then thrown upward, which KOs between 65% and 130% depending on weight and the tornado's position. In the 1P Game, knocking Link out with a tornado earns the Tornado Clear bonus, 3,000 points.

sections.name: Planet Zebes's rising acid (stage hazard)
sections.card:
Summary: A sea of acid rises and falls under Planet Zebes, the stage where Samus is fought in stage 8 of the 1P Game. Touching it does damage and high knockback, enough to KO a fighter whose damage is high.
Weak points: The acid never rises high enough to reach the topmost platform. If you are knocked into it once it has risen enough, it launches you skyward, so you can use your recovery again or simply fall back onto the stage.
Tips: A Starman or any form of strong knockback resistance makes you immune to the acid, but if you fall through it while invincible you self-destruct. Knocking Samus out with the rising acid earns the Acid Clear bonus, 1,500 points (1,000 in the Japanese version).

sections.name: Sector Z's Arwings (stage hazard)
sections.card:
Summary: Arwing fighters fly past on Sector Z, the stage where Fox is fought in stage 3 of the 1P Game, and fire lasers across the stage that deal large damage and knockback.
Weak points: Stay off the Arwings. A fighter standing on one may be KO'd if it flies offscreen to the top or side, and Arwings tend to barrel roll or fly upside down, which essentially pushes you off. The Great Fox's main guns cannot be stood on and do not fire.
Tips: Knocking Fox out with an Arwing earns the ARWING Clear bonus, 4,000 points (3,000 in the Japanese version). Sector Z is the largest stage in the game.
